content: To effectively implement sustainable health-promoting school (HPS) systems, resources must be allocated to support all components of these systems. Evidence-based practices should guide the planning and design of HPS goals, targets, and activities. This includes creating implementation plans that utilize allocated resources effectively and establishing systems for monitoring and evaluating progress. Strengthening partnerships between schools and communities is essential. This involves fostering collaborations across national, subnational, and local government departments, as well as between schools and local organizations or businesses. Such partnerships should be formalized through structured agreements and maintained through shared commitments, regular reviews, and transparent communication. The implementation of HPS systems requires clear definitions of roles and responsibilities among stakeholders, including education, health, and other relevant sectors. A multi-stakeholder committee should be established to coordinate policy development and implementation. Operational plans should outline processes for collaboration, decision-making, and communication, ensuring representation from all relevant organizations. National policies or strategies for HPS should include a rationale for coordination and approaches to identify stakeholders across government and other organizations. These policies should align with the country’s governance structure and organizational frameworks for education and health services. Shared leadership between education and health sectors is critical for sustainability, as is the involvement of international and national expertise in HPS. Developing or updating policies at national, subnational, and local levels is necessary to address health and well-being priorities in schools. Policies should explicitly address areas such as comprehensive sexuality education, violence prevention, menstrual health, life skills, nutrition, and risk factors for noncommunicable diseases. School leadership and governance practices must support a whole-school approach to HPS. This includes defining leadership models that involve students, community members, and government representatives. Leadership decisions should be informed by the needs and priorities of students, schools, and communities. Professional pathways for HPS leadership should be created or integrated into existing roles to institutionalize governance systems. Resource allocation is a critical aspect of HPS implementation. This involves reviewing current resources, aligning budgets with HPS goals, and developing flexible funding models to address local needs. Schools should have access to grants and other funding mechanisms to support health promotion activities. Teacher time for professional learning on HPS should also be prioritized. Evidence-informed practices are fundamental to planning and designing HPS activities. This requires collecting and synthesizing research to guide decision-making and establishing certification programs to formally recognize schools as health-promoting. Investing in school infrastructure is essential to create environments conducive to health and well-being. This includes providing clean facilities, safe outdoor spaces, and appropriate temperature control. Infrastructure should meet international and national guidelines and be adaptable to changing needs, such as during public health emergencies. Curriculum development should integrate health and well-being across all subjects, emphasizing life skills and health literacy. The curriculum should be flexible to incorporate new content as needed and align with international standards. Teacher training institutions play a key role in embedding HPS into education systems. Access to teacher training and professional learning is crucial for equipping educators to deliver health-promoting curricula. Training should cover topics such as mental health, sexuality education, and healthy lifestyles, using learner-centered pedagogies. Professional learning should be tailored to the needs of teachers and aligned with national standards. In summary, implementing HPS systems requires a comprehensive approach involving resource allocation, evidence-based practices, strong leadership, community partnerships, infrastructure investment, curriculum development, and teacher training.
